teaching.h: Why word order matters so much in English
teaching.p: Many languages show 'who did what' through word endings, so word order can move around freely. English mostly lost those endings, which means word order is doing almost all the work instead. That's why English sticks tightly to Subject-Verb-Object — swap the order and the meaning genuinely changes, not just the style.
teaching.ex: She reads books.

teaching.h: a vs. an — it's about sound, not spelling
teaching.p: The rule everyone half-remembers wrong: it's not about whether the next word starts with a vowel LETTER, it's about the SOUND. 'A university' sounds like it starts with 'y', so it takes 'a', not 'an' — even though u is a vowel.
teaching.ex: a university, but an hour

teaching.h: the vs. a/an — specific vs. new information
teaching.p: Use a/an the first time you introduce something, then switch to 'the' once both people know what you're talking about. This is why the same sentence can correctly use both.
teaching.ex: I saw a dog. The dog was brown.

teaching.h: When to skip the article entirely
teaching.p: When speaking generally about a whole category — not one specific example — plural and uncountable nouns often take no article at all.
teaching.ex: Dogs are loyal. I like coffee.

quiz.q: Which word order does English use?
"I saw ___ elephant at the zoo." (a/an)
Which article refers to something specific already mentioned?
Which sentence is correct for a general statement?
"She reads ___ book every night." (a)

teaching.h: Two present tenses because English separates 'always true' from 'right now'
teaching.p: Simple present is for routines and facts that stay true regardless of this exact moment. Continuous is specifically for what's happening as you speak. Mixing these up is one of the most common learner mistakes — 'I work' and 'I am working' genuinely mean different things.
teaching.ex: He works every day.

teaching.h: Continuous = be + verb-ing
teaching.p: The structure signals 'in progress right now, temporary.'
teaching.ex: He is working right now.

teaching.h: Some verbs refuse to go continuous
teaching.p: Verbs describing a state rather than an action — know, like, want, believe, own — almost never take the -ing form, even when talking about right now. 'I am knowing' sounds broken to a native ear because knowledge isn't something you do in progress, it's just a state.
teaching.ex: I know the answer, not I am knowing.

teaching.h: Full formation pattern
teaching.p: am/is/are, matched to the subject, plus the -ing form of the verb.
teaching.ex: They are studying English.

quiz.q: Which tense is used for daily habits?
"She ___ (study) English right now." (present continuous)
Which sentence is correct?
"He ___ (work) at a bank." (general fact)
The present continuous is formed with:

teaching.h: The regular pattern — and why it's not always enough
teaching.p: Adding -ed is the default rule, and it works for the vast majority of English verbs. The catch: the most common, most frequently-used verbs in English (go, see, eat, have, be) are almost all irregular, precisely because we use them so much that their old, unpredictable forms never got smoothed out over time.
teaching.ex: walk becomes walked

teaching.h: Irregular verbs just have to be memorized
teaching.p: There's no shortcut here — you learn each one individually, ideally in short phrases rather than as an isolated list.
teaching.ex: go becomes went, see becomes saw, eat becomes ate

teaching.h: "To be" in the past
teaching.p: Was for I/he/she/it, were for you/we/they.
teaching.ex: I was tired. They were happy.

teaching.h: Negating the past — a common trap
teaching.p: Once you add 'did' to a negative sentence, the main verb goes BACK to its base form — you don't double up on past tense. This is why 'I didn't went' is wrong even though it feels like it should match.
teaching.ex: I didn't go, not I didn't went.

teaching.h: The most common irregular verbs at a glance
teaching.p: These eight cover an enormous share of everyday English. Notice there's no single pattern — that's exactly why they have to be memorized as whole sets, not derived from a rule.

quiz.q: Regular past tense is formed by:
"Yesterday I ___ (go) to the market."
Which is correct?
"She ___ (be) very tired last night."
Which of these verbs is irregular?

teaching.h: Why English questions need a 'helper' word at all
teaching.p: Unlike many languages that form questions just by changing intonation or word order, English usually needs a helper verb (do/does/did) inserted at the front — this is one of the more distinctive things about English grammar.
teaching.ex: Do you like tea?

teaching.h: Past tense questions always use 'did', regardless of the original verb
teaching.p: No matter how irregular the past tense was (went, saw, ate), the question form always uses plain 'did' plus the base verb — the irregularity disappears in questions.
teaching.ex: Did you see him?

teaching.h: Negation follows the same helper-verb pattern
teaching.p: do/does/did + not, then the base form of the verb.
teaching.ex: She doesn't like coffee.

teaching.h: Wh- questions just add a question word to the front
teaching.p: Same do/does/did structure, just preceded by where/what/when/why/who.
teaching.ex: Where do you live?

quiz.q: Yes/no questions in the present tense use:
"___ you like pizza?"
Negation of "He likes tea" is:
"___ she go to the party?" (past)
In "Where do you live?", the verb "live" stays in:

teaching.h: Why prepositions are notoriously hard to learn logically
teaching.p: Prepositions rarely follow a clean rule — they're mostly memorized through exposure, which is exactly why they're one of the last things learners fully master. Still, a few patterns genuinely help.
teaching.ex: in May, on Monday, at 5pm

teaching.h: in/on/at for time — big to small
teaching.p: Think of it as zooming in: in for the biggest chunks of time (months, years), on for a specific day, at for an exact point in time.
teaching.ex: in May, on Monday, at 5pm

teaching.h: "married to" — a fixed pairing worth memorizing directly
teaching.p: This is one of those combinations native speakers never think about, but always gets 'with' from learners because it feels logical. It isn't — it's just fixed.
teaching.ex: She is married to a doctor.

teaching.h: "depend on" — another fixed pairing
teaching.p: Same story: 'depend of' feels reasonable if you're translating from certain other languages, but English fixed on 'on' for this verb specifically.
teaching.ex: It depends on the weather.

quiz.q: Which preposition is used for months?
"The meeting is ___ Monday."
Which is correct?
"It depends ___ the weather."
Which preposition is used for specific times like 5pm?

teaching.h: Why this matters beyond just labeling words
teaching.p: Knowing a word's part of speech tells you how it's allowed to behave in a sentence — where it can go, what it can pair with. This is the foundation everything else in grammar builds on.
teaching.ex: run (verb), quickly (adverb), teacher (noun)

teaching.h: Nouns and pronouns work as a team
teaching.p: Pronouns exist specifically so you don't have to keep repeating the same noun — without them, every sentence would feel painfully repetitive.
teaching.ex: The teacher graded the papers. She was tired.

teaching.h: Verbs and adjectives play very different roles
teaching.p: Verbs drive the sentence forward (the action or state); adjectives just add detail to a noun without moving anything.
teaching.ex: The tall teacher runs every morning.

teaching.h: Prepositions, conjunctions, interjections — the connective tissue
teaching.p: None of these carry meaning entirely on their own — they exist to link other words together or express a sudden reaction.
teaching.ex: Wow, she sat on the chair and read quietly.

quiz.q: In "She runs quickly," what part of speech is "quickly"?
Which word is a preposition in "The cat sat under the table"?
"He is a ___ teacher." (fill with an adjective — e.g. good)
"She" in a sentence is an example of a:
Which word class joins two clauses, like "and" or "because"?

teaching.h: Why varying sentence length actually matters
teaching.p: Native-sounding English rarely strings together only simple sentences — real writing and speech mixes short, punchy statements with longer, connected ones. Understanding these four structures is what lets you deliberately control that rhythm.
teaching.ex: The dog barked.

teaching.h: Simple sentences — one complete thought
teaching.p: Just a single independent clause: one subject, one verb, nothing attached.
teaching.ex: The dog barked.

teaching.h: Compound sentences — two equal ideas, joined
teaching.p: Two independent clauses connected by and, but, or, so, yet — both halves could stand alone if you split them.
teaching.ex: The dog barked, and the cat ran away.

teaching.h: Complex sentences — one idea depends on another
teaching.p: An independent clause plus a dependent one that can't stand by itself — the dependent clause needs the main clause to make sense.
teaching.ex: Because it was raining, we stayed inside.

teaching.h: Compound-complex — combining both patterns at once
teaching.p: This is what genuinely sophisticated writing often looks like: a dependent clause attached to a full compound sentence.
teaching.ex: Because it was raining, we stayed inside, and we watched a movie.

quiz.q: "The dog barked." is a:
A compound sentence needs a:
options: coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses
quiz.answer: coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses

quiz.q: "Because it was raining, we stayed inside." is a:
"The dog barked, ___ the cat ran away." (coordinating conjunction)
A dependent clause:
options: can stand alone as a full sentence
cannot stand alone as a full sentence
quiz.answer: cannot stand alone as a full sentence

teaching.h: The core rule, and why it trips people up in longer sentences
teaching.p: Singular subject, singular verb; plural subject, plural verb. This feels obvious in short sentences, but gets genuinely tricky once other words sit between the subject and the verb, tempting you to match the wrong noun.
teaching.ex: The student studies. The students study.

teaching.h: "And" almost always makes it plural
teaching.p: Two subjects joined by 'and' are treated as a combined plural, even if each one is individually singular.
teaching.ex: Tom and Jerry are friends.

teaching.h: "Or"/"nor" — the verb listens to the closer subject
teaching.p: This is the genuinely counterintuitive one: when subjects are joined by or/nor, the verb matches whichever subject is physically closest to it, not the first one.
teaching.ex: Neither the teacher nor the students are ready.

teaching.h: Indefinite pronouns sound plural but grammatically aren't
teaching.p: Everyone, each, somebody, nobody all take a SINGULAR verb, even though they seem to describe a group of people.
teaching.ex: Everyone is here.

quiz.q: "The student ___ (study) every night."
"Tom and Jerry ___ (be) friends."
"Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready." (verb agrees with which subject?)
"Everyone ___ (be) here."
Which verb form is correct: "Each of the boys ___ a book."

teaching.h: Why English has twelve tenses instead of three
teaching.p: English doesn't just mark WHEN something happens — it separately marks whether it's a simple fact, an ongoing process, a completed action, or a completed-and-ongoing mix. Multiply 4 aspects by 3 time periods (past/present/future) and you get the full 12-tense grid.
teaching.ex: I work. I am working. I have worked. I have been working.

teaching.h: The past follows the exact same four-way split
teaching.p: Simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous — same logic, just shifted to the past.
teaching.ex: I worked. I was working. I had worked. I had been working.

teaching.h: The future too
teaching.p: Same four-way pattern, now with 'will' involved.
teaching.ex: I will work. I will be working. I will have worked.

teaching.h: The practical shortcut for choosing the right one
teaching.p: Ask yourself: is this happening right now, already finished, still ongoing up to now, or yet to happen? That single question narrows you down to the right tense almost every time, faster than memorizing all 12 forms as a flat list.

quiz.q: "I have worked here for five years." is which tense?
"By next year, I ___ (will/graduate)." (future simple)
"I was working when she called." is which tense?
"She ___ (had/finish) her homework before dinner." (past perfect)
Which tense describes an action still ongoing up to now?

teaching.h: Four conditionals, four different relationships to reality
teaching.p: Each conditional signals how likely or real the situation is — from 'always true' facts through 'realistic future,' 'unlikely hypothetical,' down to 'impossible, because the past already happened.' Once you see them as a scale of realness, they stop feeling arbitrary.
teaching.ex: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

teaching.h: First conditional — genuinely possible futures
teaching.p: If + present simple, will + base verb — used when there's a real, reasonable chance the condition happens.
teaching.ex: If it rains, I will bring an umbrella.

teaching.h: Second conditional — imagining something unlikely or untrue right now
teaching.p: If + past simple, would + base verb. Using past tense here doesn't mean past TIME — it's a grammatical signal for 'this isn't real.'
teaching.ex: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.

teaching.h: Third conditional — the past you can't change
teaching.p: If + past perfect, would have + past participle — imagining a different outcome for something that already, unchangeably, happened.
teaching.ex: If I had studied, I would have passed.

quiz.q: "If you heat water to 100°C, it boils." is which conditional?
"If it rains, I ___ (will/bring) an umbrella." (first conditional)
"If I won the lottery, I would travel." describes:
"If I ___ (had/study), I would have passed." (third conditional)
The third conditional talks about:
options: an imagined outcome of the unchangeable past
quiz.answer: an imagined outcome of the unchangeable past

teaching.h: Why this distinction is worth learning explicitly
teaching.p: Recognizing phrases vs. clauses is the key to fixing one of the most common writing errors: the sentence fragment (mistaking a phrase or dependent clause for a complete sentence).
teaching.ex: in the morning, running quickly, a big red house

teaching.h: A clause always has both a subject and a verb
teaching.p: That subject-verb pairing is the one test that separates a clause from a phrase, every time.
teaching.ex: she runs, because he was late

teaching.h: Independent clauses are complete on their own
teaching.p: If it has a subject, a verb, and expresses a full thought, it can stand alone as its own sentence.
teaching.ex: She runs every morning.

teaching.h: Dependent clauses have the pieces but not the independence
teaching.p: They technically have a subject and verb, but a connector word (because, although, when) makes them incomplete without a main clause attached.
teaching.ex: because he was late (incomplete on its own)

quiz.q: "in the morning" is an example of a:
"she runs" is an example of a:
The key difference between a phrase and a clause is:
options: a clause has a subject and verb, a phrase doesn't
quiz.answer: a clause has a subject and verb, a phrase doesn't

quiz.q: "Because he was late" is a:
An independent clause:
options: can stand alone as a complete sentence
quiz.answer: can stand alone as a complete sentence

teaching.h: Active voice — the natural default
teaching.p: The subject performs the action. Most confident, direct English writing leans active voice by default.
teaching.ex: The chef cooked the meal.

teaching.h: Passive voice — flipping the focus
teaching.p: The subject now receives the action instead of doing it, built with a form of 'be' plus the past participle.
teaching.ex: The meal was cooked by the chef.

teaching.h: When passive actually earns its place
teaching.p: Use it deliberately when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or you specifically want to emphasize what happened to something rather than who did it — not just as a random stylistic choice.
teaching.ex: The window was broken. (we don't know or care who did it)

teaching.h: Only the 'be' verb changes across tenses
teaching.p: The past participle itself stays frozen; only the helper verb shifts to match the tense.
teaching.ex: The meal is cooked. The meal was cooked. The meal will be cooked.

quiz.q: "The chef cooked the meal." is:
Change to passive: "The meal ___ (be) cooked by the chef."
Passive voice is useful when:
options: the doer is unknown or unimportant
you want to be as direct as possible
quiz.answer: the doer is unknown or unimportant

quiz.q: Passive voice is formed with:
"The window ___ (be) broken." (passive, past simple)

teaching.h: Direct speech preserves the exact words
teaching.p: Quotation marks signal 'these are the precise words someone said', unchanged.
teaching.ex: She said, "I am tired."

teaching.h: Indirect speech reports the idea, from a shifted viewpoint
teaching.p: No quotation marks, and crucially, the tense usually shifts one step further into the past — because you're now speaking from a later point in time than when the words were originally said.
teaching.ex: She said that she was tired.

teaching.h: The backshift pattern, explained
teaching.p: Present simple slides to past simple, present continuous slides to past continuous — the whole system shifts back by one tense to reflect that time has passed since the original statement.
teaching.ex: "I am working" becomes: She said she was working.

teaching.h: Pronouns and time words shift too, for the same reason
teaching.p: "I" often becomes "she/he" and "today" often becomes "that day" — everything realigns to the new speaker's perspective and the new point in time.
teaching.ex: "I will come today" becomes: He said he would come that day.

quiz.q: "She said, 'I am tired.'" is:
Report this: "I am tired" → She said that she ___ tired. (was)
In reported speech, present simple usually shifts to:
"I will come today" reported becomes: He said he ___ (will/come) that day.
Indirect speech uses:
options: quotation marks around the exact words
no quotation marks, tense often shifted
quiz.answer: no quotation marks, tense often shifted

teaching.h: Commas: the pause that changes meaning, not just rhythm
teaching.p: Beyond just separating list items, a comma before a coordinating conjunction (and, but) joining two full independent clauses is what keeps long sentences from becoming confusing run-ons.
teaching.ex: I bought apples, bread, and milk. She was tired, but she kept working.

teaching.h: Apostrophes have exactly two jobs — and 'plural' isn't one of them
teaching.p: Contractions (don't, it's) and possession (the dog's leash) are the only correct uses. Using an apostrophe to make a plain plural — 'apple's for sale' — is one of the most common English writing errors, in native and non-native writing alike.
teaching.ex: The dog's leash was chewed. It's raining. (correct)

teaching.h: The three things that always get capitalized
teaching.p: The first word of a sentence, every proper noun, and the pronoun 'I' — always, with no exceptions, even mid-sentence.
teaching.ex: My friend John and I visited London.

teaching.h: Semicolons and colons — related but distinct jobs
teaching.p: A semicolon connects two closely related independent clauses without needing a conjunction. A colon specifically introduces something — a list, an explanation, an elaboration.
teaching.ex: She was exhausted; she kept working anyway. Bring these: a pen, paper, and a laptop.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: I bought apples bread and milk.
I bought apples, bread, and milk.
quiz.answer: I bought apples, bread, and milk.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
"My friend John and ___ visited London." (always capitalized)
A colon is used to:
A semicolon can join two:

teaching.h: Gerunds vs. infinitives — why some verbs demand one or the other
teaching.p: There's no universal logic here; certain verbs (enjoy, avoid, finish) simply require the -ing gerund form after them, while others (want, decide, hope) require 'to' + base verb. This gets learned per-verb, through exposure, more than through a single rule.
teaching.ex: I enjoy swimming. (gerund) I want to swim. (infinitive)

teaching.h: Relative clauses add detail without starting a new sentence
teaching.p: who/which/that/whose let you attach extra information about a noun directly, instead of breaking it into two separate sentences.
teaching.ex: The woman who called earlier is my teacher.

teaching.h: Phrasal verbs — where the meaning isn't in the individual words
teaching.p: This is genuinely one of the hardest parts of English for learners, because you can know every individual word and still not guess the combined meaning. 'Give up' has nothing literal to do with 'giving' or 'up' — it just means to quit.
teaching.ex: give up (quit), look after (take care of), run into (meet by chance)

teaching.h: The subjunctive — a quiet, easy-to-miss mood
teaching.p: Used for wishes, suggestions, and hypotheticals, this mood often uses the base verb form regardless of the subject — which is why 'I suggest that he arrive early' sounds slightly unusual but is actually correct.
teaching.ex: I suggest that he arrive early. If I were you, I would rest.

quiz.q: "I enjoy swimming." uses a:
"The woman ___ called earlier is my teacher." (relative pronoun)
"Give up" is an example of a:
"If I ___ you, I would rest." (subjunctive)
The subjunctive mood is typically used for:

teaching.h: Why these words are what make writing feel connected
teaching.p: Without transitions, a paragraph is just a pile of separate facts. Transitional devices explicitly signal HOW one idea relates to the next — contrast, cause, addition, sequence — which is exactly what makes writing read smoothly instead of choppily.
teaching.ex: however, therefore, in addition, for example

teaching.h: Signaling contrast
teaching.p: however, on the other hand, and nevertheless all flag that what's coming pushes against the previous idea.
teaching.ex: She studied hard. However, she still felt nervous.

teaching.h: Signaling cause and result
teaching.p: therefore, as a result, and consequently all connect a cause directly to its effect.
teaching.ex: It rained heavily. As a result, the game was cancelled.

teaching.h: Adding ideas and sequencing steps
teaching.p: furthermore and in addition stack on a related point; first, next, finally organize steps in order — both make multi-part explanations far easier to follow.
teaching.ex: First, preheat the oven. Next, mix the ingredients.

quiz.q: Which word signals contrast?
"It rained heavily. ___, the game was cancelled." (cause/result)
"Furthermore" is used to:
"___, preheat the oven." (sequencing word for the first step)
Transitional devices mainly help with:
